title: Reading Input with Scanner
description: Asking a question and storing whatever the person types.

content.value: Until now every value was typed into the code before it ran. A `Scanner` reads what a person types at the keyboard, so the same program can give a different answer each time.

content.title: One sample run
content.outro: Read with `nextLine()` instead and `age + 1` would join text: a 10 year old would be told they will be 101.

content.value: If the person types something that is not a number, `nextInt()` stops the program with an `InputMismatchException`. Checking input needs decisions: that is the next module.
`nextInt()` reads the digits and stops. The invisible Enter key is left waiting. The next `nextLine()` finds it and returns empty text without waiting.

steps.label: nextLine()
steps.detail: Sees the Enter at once: returns `""`

content.title: Where the Enter goes
content.caption: The person typed `14` then Enter. Only the digits were taken.

items.title: Swallow the Enter
items.text: One extra `nextLine()` throws the leftover Enter away.

items.title: Text first
items.code:

int age = scanner.nextInt();
items.text: Ask text questions before number ones. No `nextLine()` follows a `nextInt()`.

content.question: You type `14` for `nextInt()`. What does the very next `nextLine()` give back?
content.explain: The leftover Enter is still in the queue, so `nextLine()` stops at once with nothing in it.

content.value: Sometimes you already have text that holds digits. Module 2's `Integer.parseInt` (and `Double.parseDouble`) turns it into a real number.

content.caption: Sample run: type `3` and it prints `That will be 750 rupees.` Reading a line and then parsing avoids the leftover Enter trap completely, which is why many real programs do it.

content.question: Which line turns the text `"42"` into a number?
content.explain: `Integer.parseInt` reads digits in text and gives back an `int`. A cast cannot turn text into a number.

quiz.question: What does `scanner.nextLine()` give back?
options: A String: everything typed up to the Enter key.
An int, if the person typed digits.
quiz.explain: `nextLine()` always hands back text. If you need a number from it, read with `nextInt()` instead or parse the text afterwards.

quiz.question: Why use `System.out.print` rather than `println` for a question?
options: The cursor stays on the same line, so the answer is typed next to the question.
`println` cannot be used before a Scanner.
It makes the Scanner wait longer.
quiz.explain: `print` leaves the cursor where it is. With `println` the person types their answer on the line below, which looks wrong.

quiz.question: A 10 year old types 10, read with `nextLine()` into a String called `age`. What does `System.out.println(age + 1)` print?
options: 101, because joining text puts the 1 on the end
quiz.explain: `nextLine()` gives text, and `+` joins text rather than adding. Reading with `nextInt()` gives a real number, so `age + 1` would be 11.

quiz.question: Why does a `nextLine()` straight after a `nextInt()` come back empty?
options: `nextInt()` leaves the Enter key in the queue, and `nextLine()` reads up to it.
`nextLine()` can only be used once per program.
The Scanner has run out of input.
quiz.explain: `nextInt()` takes the digits but not the Enter that follows them. The next `nextLine()` finds that leftover Enter and decides the line has already ended.

quiz.question: What is the simplest way to avoid that trap?
options: Ask the text questions before the number questions.
quiz.explain: The problem only happens when a `nextLine()` follows a `nextInt()`. Reordering the questions, or adding one extra `scanner.nextLine()` to swallow the Enter, both fix it.
